transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I spend so much time trying to fix how I look before I go out that I end up missing things with my family and at work. My primary care doctor recommended I come in because it's starting to really damage my relationships and my job.
Can you tell me more about what specifically you try to fix about your appearance that takes up so much of your time?

I'm deeply self-conscious about my face, particularly feeling like my nose is crooked, my skin is saggy and blotchy, and my jaw is drooping. Before I can leave the house, I'll spend hours trying to fix it by constantly changing my clothes, adjusting the lighting, checking photos of myself, and asking others if I look okay.
Do you ever experience repetitive thoughts or urges to perform specific rituals, like checking or asking for reassurance, that are directly related to your concerns about your appearance?

Yes, I get these overwhelming urges and find myself trapped in those rituals constantly. Before work or seeing my kids, I'll spend over an hour changing shirts, adjusting the lights, zooming in on photos, and asking my daughter or coworkers if my face looks weird or if my jaw is drooping. I keep fussing with it until I get so worked up that I end up late or just cancel entirely.
Can you describe how much of your time is spent on these appearance concerns versus the time spent on the repetitive behaviors or rituals you feel compelled to perform?

Honestly, both take up a massive amount of my day and are closely linked. The worries about my crooked nose and saggy skin are constantly on my mind, but I'll also spend an hour or more before every shift or family visit actively doing rituals like changing shirts, adjusting the lights, and zooming in on photos.
Do you believe your perceived flaws, such as your nose being crooked or skin being saggy, are actually noticeable to others, or are they only a concern to you?

Even though my family and coworkers tell me I look fine for my age, I am completely convinced these flaws are highly noticeable to everyone. I feel like an older, lopsided guy who stands out in a bad way at the front of the restaurant, which is why I'm constantly asking my daughter and coworkers for reassurance about whether my face looks weird.

When you're performing these rituals, such as checking your appearance or asking for reassurance, are you primarily trying to reduce anxiety about your appearance, or are you trying to prevent some other kind of harm or bad outcome from happening?

I'm really just trying to reduce the intense anxiety I feel about my appearance and make myself look acceptable before anyone else sees me. I'm not trying to prevent some external disaster or physical harm; it's entirely about the overwhelming worry that I'll look "off" or lopsided in public and in photos. I just keep fussing to try and stop feeling so incredibly self-conscious.
Can you clarify if your main distress comes from the intrusive thoughts about your appearance or from the feeling that you must perform these rituals to alleviate your anxiety about how you look?

It is really a painful cycle where both feed into each other, starting with the constant thoughts that my face looks crooked and saggy. That intense anxiety forces me into exhausting rituals, like endlessly changing my shirt and checking photos, to try and fix how I look. While the thoughts are deeply upsetting, it’s those endless rituals that ultimately make me late, force me to cancel plans, and are ruining my job and family life.
Do you think you would still feel the need to perform these rituals if you didn't have these concerns about your appearance, or are the rituals and appearance concerns inextricably linked for you?

They are completely linked for me. I only do all this checking, changing, and asking for reassurance because of how worried I am about my face looking crooked or saggy. If I didn't have those intense concerns about my appearance, I wouldn't feel any need to do these rituals at all.

Can you tell me if there are times when you feel like you can ignore these thoughts about your appearance and not perform the rituals, or do you feel an overwhelming urge to act on them every time they occur?

I feel an overwhelming urge to act on these thoughts and simply cannot ignore them. Before work or seeing my kids, I get completely caught up in rituals like changing shirts, checking the mirror, and asking for reassurance. I keep fussing with my appearance until I'm too worked up and late, rather than being able to just brush the thoughts aside.
Have you ever experienced any other types of obsessive thoughts or compulsions that are not related to your appearance, such as fears of contamination, symmetry, or harm coming to others?
No, I don't have any fears like that about contamination, symmetry, or harm. My worries and habits are strictly focused on my appearance and how my face looks to other people.
Can you tell me if you have ever had any obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors that are not related to your appearance, or have your symptoms always been focused on how you look?

My symptoms have always been entirely focused on my appearance, specifically my face, nose, skin, and jaw. I have never experienced other types of obsessions or compulsions like excessive cleaning, checking locks, or counting. For me, the struggle has always just been about how I look.

Can you describe any instances where you felt like you had to repeat a specific behavior, like checking or grooming, a certain number of times, or in a very specific way, in order to feel like you've done it 'correctly' or to reduce your anxiety about your appearance?

Yes, before every shift or seeing my kids, I get stuck in this exhausting loop where I spend over an hour changing shirts repeatedly, adjusting the bathroom lighting, and zooming in on photos of myself. I also feel compelled to keep asking my daughter or coworkers if my face looks weird or if my jaw is drooping just to try and feel some relief. I keep fussing with everything to get it to look "right" until I'm so worked up and late that I sometimes just cancel going out entirely.

Do you think your excessive focus on your appearance and the rituals you perform to try to improve it are more distressing to you, or is it the fact that you feel compelled to repeat these behaviors in a specific way that's causing you the most distress?

My distress is definitely driven by my intense worry about how I look and my desperate attempts to fix my appearance so it looks acceptable. I'm not repeating these actions out of a rigid need to perform a specific ritual in a certain order. Rather, I am constantly trying to check, adjust, and "fix" my face and clothes until I feel presentable enough to be seen in public.

Can you estimate what percentage of your daily thoughts are preoccupied with concerns about your appearance, versus the percentage of time spent on the actual compulsive behaviors like checking or rituals?

I'm not really sure of the exact percentages or how to split them up. I just know that both the constant worrying thoughts and the physical rituals take up an overwhelming amount of my day. It feels like they completely consume almost all of my time.
Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning that is not directly related to your appearance concerns?

I don't think I have any other major areas of distress or impairment that aren't connected to my appearance worries. Almost all of my current struggles, whether it's problems at my job or missing events with my family, seem to stem directly from how much I worry about how I look.

Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any obsessive thoughts or compulsions that you feel are irrational or excessive, but are not directly related to your appearance, such as fear of germs or a need for symmetry?

No, I have never experienced those kinds of obsessive thoughts or compulsions, like worrying about germs or needing things to be symmetrical. My worries and repetitive behaviors are strictly focused on my appearance and how my face looks to others.
Do you think your main issue is the excessive time and effort you spend trying to improve your appearance, or is it the recurring, intrusive thoughts about your appearance that drive your behaviors?

It is definitely a combination of both. The constant, distressing thoughts about my face looking crooked, old, and saggy are what trigger the overwhelming urge to spend hours checking the mirror, changing clothes, and trying to fix my appearance, which ultimately causes me to be late or cancel my plans.
Can you think of any situation where your obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors would be driven by concerns other than your appearance, or are your symptoms exclusively related to how you look?

My worries and behaviors are exclusively related to how I look, specifically my face, nose, skin, and jaw. I've never had any of these obsessive thoughts or rituals about other things like cleanliness, order, or safety. For me, it is always entirely about my appearance and how other people perceive me.
Do you think your life would be significantly improved if you could just stop having these intrusive thoughts about your appearance, even if you still felt compelled to perform some of the rituals?

Yes, getting rid of those intrusive thoughts would be a massive relief because they are what drive my anxiety and the rituals in the first place. Even if some of the behaviors remained, not having that constant mental torment and self-consciousness would dramatically improve my life. It would really help reduce the panic that always makes me cancel plans and miss out on work and family.

Do you believe that if your appearance concerns were somehow resolved, you would still feel the urge to perform these rituals, or are the rituals entirely a response to your distress about your appearance?

The rituals are entirely a response to the distress over my appearance. If I felt like my face and body looked "right" or acceptable, I wouldn't feel any need to spend hours changing shirts, adjusting the lighting, or asking others for reassurance. These behaviors are solely my attempt to fix or cope with how "off" I feel I look.

Can you think of any situation or time in your life where you had obsessive thoughts or compulsive behaviors that were not related to your appearance, or have all your obsessive thoughts and compulsions always been about how you look?

No, I can't recall ever having these kinds of obsessions or compulsions about anything else in my life. My obsessive thoughts and repetitive behaviors have always been focused entirely on my appearance, like my face, my skin, and how I look in photos. I've never struggled with these kinds of worries over non-appearance-related things.
Do you think your main problem is the obsessive thoughts and compulsions themselves, or is it the distress and impairment they cause in your daily life due to your appearance concerns?

While the constant thoughts and grooming rituals are incredibly exhausting, it is the actual real-world consequences that are the most painful and forced me to get help. Missing my daughter's school events, getting written up at work, and losing my family's trust because I'm hiding away trying to fix my face is what is truly devastating.
Do you think your appearance concerns would improve if you could stop performing the rituals, or do you believe the rituals are necessary to temporarily alleviate your distress about your appearance?

I haven't really thought about it in those terms, to be honest. In the moment, I just feel this overwhelming urge to try and fix how I look, even though it usually just ends up making me more anxious, worked up, and late. Because of that, I'm really not sure if stopping the rituals would actually help my worries or if they are truly necessary for me to cope.

If you were to stop performing these rituals and trying to fix your appearance, do you think the intrusive thoughts about your appearance would continue to cause you significant distress, or would the distress primarily come from the fact that you're not performing the rituals?

I'm not really sure, because I've never actually been able to stop myself from doing the rituals to find out. I haven't thought about whether the distress would come from the thoughts themselves or just from not being able to try and fix how I look. It all just feels like one big ball of anxiety to me.

If you were able to completely ignore your appearance concerns for a day, do you think you would still feel the urge to perform any of these rituals, such as checking or repeating behaviors, for reasons unrelated to your appearance?

No, I wouldn't feel any urge to do them at all if I could ignore my appearance concerns. All of those behaviors—like changing shirts, adjusting the lighting, zooming in on photos, and asking for reassurance—are entirely driven by my anxiety about how my face and body look. Without those worries, I wouldn't do any of those things.
